title: Blood Supply, Lymph Drainage, and Innervation of the Reproductive Organs and Breast
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the arteries, veins, lymphatics, and nerves of the gonads, uterus, external genitalia, perineum, and breast. Most of the anatomy is explained by two rules: the gonads keep the vessels they had high on the posterior abdominal wall before they descended, and lymph tends to follow the arteries back to their origin. Board questions turn these rules into predictions: which side gets a varicocele, which structure a pelvic clamp can catch, where a tumor spreads first, which nerve fails after a pelvic operation, and where to find the pudendal nerve. Learn the route of each vessel and nerve and the clinical findings follow from it.

Pelvic organ position, broad ligament, and perineal boundaries (RE-2, RE-4)

Gonadal descent and the formation of the inguinal canal (RE-1)

connections.how: Gonadal descent from the upper lumbar region explains why gonadal vessels and lymph run to the aorta and para-aortic nodes.
The nerves described here carry out the male sexual response, and the uterine spiral arteries drive menstruation.
The ureter's course under the uterine artery and the left renal vein's role in varicocele link the pelvis to the kidney.
First nodal sites for testicular, ovarian, cervical, vulvar, and breast cancers follow the lymph routes taught here.
Alpha-1 receptors in the bladder neck and cGMP in cavernosal smooth muscle explain drug effects on emission and erection.

terms.def: A network of about 8 to 12 veins in the spermatic cord that surrounds the testicular artery, cools arterial blood, and drains into the testicular vein.
Dilation and tortuosity of the pampiniform plexus caused by raised venous pressure or valve failure in the testicular vein.
Condensed connective tissue at the base of the broad ligament that carries the uterine vessels from the pelvic wall to the cervix.
Lymph nodes around the abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava that receive lymph from the gonads, kidneys, and pelvic node chains.
Nodes in the subcutaneous tissue below the inguinal ligament that drain the skin of the lower trunk, perineum, and lower limb.
The first lymph node to receive lymph from a tumor site, and therefore the first expected to contain metastasis.
Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers from the ventral rami of S2 to S4 that supply the pelvic organs and erectile tissue.
Sympathetic nerves that connect the superior hypogastric plexus to the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus on each side.
Sympathetically driven movement of sperm and glandular secretions into the prostatic urethra with closure of the bladder neck.
Somatic nerve from S2 to S4 that supplies the skin and striated muscles of the perineum, including the external urethral and anal sphincters.
A fascial tunnel on the medial surface of the obturator internus that carries the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels to the perineum.
Nodes along the internal thoracic vessels beside the sternum that drain the medial breast and anterior chest wall.

sections.title: Gonadal arteries and veins, and why varicocele favors the left

blocks.text: The testes and ovaries develop on the posterior abdominal wall at about the level of the upper lumbar vertebrae and take their blood vessels with them as they descend. Both gonadal arteries therefore arise from the anterolateral abdominal aorta at about L2, just below the renal arteries. Each runs down and laterally behind the peritoneum, crossing anterior to the ureter.

The testicular artery enters the deep inguinal ring and runs in the spermatic cord to the testis. The testis also receives the artery to the ductus deferens (from a vesical branch of the internal iliac) and the cremasteric artery (from the inferior epigastric), which anastomose with it. The ovarian artery crosses the pelvic brim in the suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament and anastomoses with the uterine artery in the broad ligament, so the ovary and uterus share a dual supply.

Venous drainage begins in the pampiniform plexus, which wraps around the testicular artery in the cord. Cooler venous blood draws heat from the arterial blood (countercurrent heat exchange), helping keep the testis about 2 to 3 °C (about 4 to 5 °F) below core temperature, which spermatogenesis requires. The plexus narrows to a single testicular vein near the deep ring. The two veins then end differently: the right vein enters the inferior vena cava (IVC) directly at an acute, oblique angle, while the longer left vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle. The ovarian veins follow the same pattern.

blocks.title: Right versus left gonadal veins
rows: Left renal vein can be compressed between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta
Uncommon; isolated or nonreducing cases suggest obstruction
blocks.caption: Anatomical differences that raise venous pressure on the left.

blocks.title: Why a left varicocele impairs fertility
steps: Long left vein enters left renal vein at right angle
Higher hydrostatic pressure and absent or incompetent valves
Reflux dilates the pampiniform plexus
Countercurrent cooling fails and testicular temperature rises
Germ cell damage lowers sperm count and motility
blocks.caption: Causal chain from left-sided venous anatomy to impaired spermatogenesis.

blocks.text: A varicocele feels like a bag of worms above the testis, enlarges with standing or a Valsalva maneuver, and collapses when the patient lies down because gravity no longer opposes drainage. It is found in about 15% of adult men and is more common in men with infertility, where warming of the testis, local hypoxia, and oxidative stress are thought to damage germ cells; the affected testis may be smaller. A varicocele that appears suddenly, does not empty when supine, or is isolated on the right points to obstruction: a left renal tumor with renal vein thrombus blocks left gonadal outflow, and a retroperitoneal mass or IVC obstruction can do the same on the right. The female counterpart of venous reflux is pelvic congestion from dilated ovarian veins.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the side of a varicocele
blocks.text: A 62-year-old man develops a new left scrotal swelling over a few weeks, with hematuria and flank pain. The veins stay full when he lies down. A varicocele in an older man that does not empty supine is not a valve problem, because a valve-failure varicocele drains when gravity is removed. The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, so a left renal cell carcinoma growing into the renal vein raises pressure in the gonadal vein and backs blood into the pampiniform plexus. The same finding on the right would point to IVC obstruction, because the right vein drains directly into the IVC.

sections.title: The uterine artery and its relation to the ureter

blocks.text: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, often near the umbilical artery. It runs medially across the pelvic floor in the base of the broad ligament, within the cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament, toward the cervix. Near the supravaginal cervix, at about the level of the internal os, it gives a cervicovaginal branch and turns sharply upward. It then climbs, tortuous, along the lateral margin of the uterus between the layers of the broad ligament and ends by anastomosing with the ovarian artery near the uterine horn, sending tubal and ovarian branches.

Inside the myometrium the uterine artery gives arcuate arteries, then radial arteries, which become straight arteries to the basal endometrium and coiled spiral arteries to the functional layer. Only the spiral arteries respond to ovarian hormones, which is why the functional layer is shed at menstruation while the basal layer survives (RE-6). Uterine veins form a plexus beside the uterus and vagina that drains to the internal iliac veins.
Where the ureter is at risk

The ureter enters the pelvis by crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, descends on the lateral pelvic wall in front of the internal iliac artery and behind the ovary, then turns medially through the base of the broad ligament toward the bladder. In that medial course it passes beneath the uterine artery about 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix, just above the lateral vaginal fornix. The artery crosses above it like a bridge over water. A clamp or ligature placed on the uterine vessels at this point can include or cut the ureter. A second site of risk is the pelvic brim, where the ureter lies just behind the ovarian vessels in the suspensory ligament.

blocks.title: Mechanisms of ureteric injury near the uterine artery
rows: Lumen closed by suture or clamp
Hydronephrosis, flank pain; bilateral ligation gives anuria and rising creatinine
Urine leak into the pelvis (urinoma), fever, ileus, rising serum creatinine as leaked urine is reabsorbed
Delayed necrosis after days to weeks, then a ureterovaginal fistula
blocks.caption: Each pattern follows from what was done to the ureter at the crossing.

blocks.text: Devascularization deserves emphasis because it is delayed. The ureter has no single artery; it is supplied segmentally by small branches that run longitudinally in its adventitia. The abdominal ureter receives branches from the medial side (renal, gonadal, aortic), but the pelvic ureter receives them from the lateral side (internal iliac, vesical, and uterine branches). Stripping the pelvic ureter from its lateral attachments can leave a segment ischemic, and a fistula to the vagina presents as continuous leakage of urine with otherwise normal voiding. Unilateral obstruction may be clinically silent at first because the other kidney maintains the glomerular filtration rate.

sections.title: Lymph drainage of the reproductive organs and predicting nodal spread

blocks.text: Lymphatic vessels usually travel with the arteries that supply an organ and drain back toward the origin of those arteries. Applying this rule predicts the first nodal station for most reproductive tumors. The gonads draw their arteries from the aorta at about L2, so testicular and ovarian lymph runs up the gonadal vessels to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near the renal veins, skipping the pelvis and groin. Pelvic organs supplied by internal iliac branches drain to the iliac nodes on the pelvic wall. Skin and surface mucosa of the perineum below the hymen drain, like all skin below the umbilicus, to the superficial inguinal nodes.

rows: Para-aortic (lumbar), at about L1 to L2

Follow ovarian vessels in the suspensory ligament
Mainly external iliac; fundus also para-aortic
Lymph runs along the round ligament
Internal and external iliac (including obturator) and sacral
Follow uterine vessels in the cardinal ligament
Lower vagina below the hymen, vulva
Deep inguinal, some to external iliac
Deeper erectile tissue drains below the fascia lata
blocks.caption: Pelvic and para-aortic stations drain upward to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct; inguinal nodes drain to the external iliac nodes.

blocks.text: The most tested contrast is the testis versus the scrotum. A testicular germ cell tumor spreads first to retroperitoneal para-aortic nodes, the right testis mainly to interaortocaval nodes and the left mainly to left para-aortic nodes just below the left renal vein. An enlarged inguinal node is not expected from a testicular tumor unless the tumor has invaded the scrotal skin or the scrotum has been surgically breached, which opens a route into skin lymphatics. In contrast, squamous cell carcinoma of the scrotal skin spreads first to superficial inguinal nodes. Because retroperitoneal nodes drain into the thoracic duct, advanced testicular cancer can enlarge the left supraclavicular node.

In women, ovarian cancer reaches para-aortic nodes directly, although its dominant spread is across the peritoneal surface. Cervical cancer spreads laterally through the cardinal ligament to pelvic nodes before para-aortic nodes, so involvement of para-aortic nodes indicates more advanced disease. Vulvar cancer goes first to superficial inguinal nodes, and lesions near the midline or clitoris can drain to both groins. Vaginal tumors drain according to their level: upper third to iliac nodes and lower third to inguinal nodes.

blocks.title: Worked example: matching the node to the tumor
blocks.text: A 30-year-old man has a firm, painless testicular mass and a palpable inguinal node. The testis drains along its vessels to para-aortic nodes, so the inguinal node does not fit testicular spread unless the scrotal skin is involved. The next question is whether another skin or perineal source drains to that groin: scrotal skin, penile skin, the lower anal canal, or the lower limb. For the testicular mass itself, the first station to examine is the retroperitoneum at about the level of the renal veins. Applying the arterial origin rule (aorta for the gonads, internal iliac for pelvic viscera, skin to the groin) separates these possibilities before any imaging.

blocks.predict: Predict the first nodal station for a tumor of the lower third of the vagina and for one of the cervix.
blocks.explain: The lower vagina is surface tissue below the hymen and drains with perineal skin; the cervix drains with the uterine vessels to the pelvic wall.

sections.title: Autonomic and somatic nerves of the male sexual response

blocks.text: The male sexual response runs in three phases, each controlled by a different division of the nervous system: erection by parasympathetic fibers, emission by sympathetic fibers, and ejaculation by the somatic pudendal nerve acting on striated perineal muscle. Knowing which pathway runs each phase lets you predict which phase fails after a given injury.

blocks.title: Three phases, three divisions
rows: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4), inferior hypogastric plexus, cavernous nerves
Nitric oxide relaxes helicine arteries and trabecular smooth muscle
Lower thoracic and upper lumbar cord (about T11 to L2), lumbar splanchnic nerves, superior hypogastric plexus, hypogastric nerves
Alpha-1 contraction of epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate; bladder neck closes
Pudendal nerve (S2 to S4), perineal branch
Rhythmic contraction of bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus expels semen
blocks.caption: Detumescence after ejaculation is sympathetic: norepinephrine contracts cavernosal smooth muscle through alpha-1 receptors.

blocks.title: Molecular mechanism of erection
steps: Cavernous nerves and endothelium release nitric oxide
Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase
cGMP rises and activates protein kinase G
Cytosolic Ca2+ falls; smooth muscle relaxes
Arterial inflow fills cavernous sinusoids
Expanding sinusoids compress subtunical veins against tunica albuginea
Venous outflow is trapped; the penis becomes rigid
blocks.caption: Phosphodiesterase type 5 ends the signal by degrading cGMP, which is why blocking it prolongs smooth muscle relaxation.

blocks.text: Erection begins with nitric oxide from nonadrenergic noncholinergic nerve terminals and is sustained by endothelial nitric oxide; acetylcholine contributes mainly by stimulating endothelial release. Arterial blood reaches the corpora through the deep arteries of the penis, branches of the internal pudendal artery. Erection is primarily a vascular event, because rigidity depends on high inflow and closure of venous outflow (veno-occlusion), and either arterial disease or a leaky venous mechanism can defeat it. Erection can be reflexogenic, through a sacral reflex arc carried by the dorsal nerve of the penis to S2 to S4, or psychogenic, from the brain. Men with spinal cord injury above the sacral segments often keep reflex erections, while sacral cord or cavernous nerve damage abolishes them.

Emission loads semen into the prostatic urethra. At the same time sympathetic tone through alpha-1 receptors closes the bladder neck (internal urethral sphincter), so that when the pudendal nerve fires the bulbospongiosus, semen can only go forward through the spongy urethra. The external urethral sphincter relaxes during expulsion. The whole sequence is coordinated by spinal reflex centers in the lumbosacral cord under brain modulation.

blocks.title: Predicting failure from the injured pathway
rows: Cavernous nerve damage in radical pelvic surgery (nerves run posterolateral to the prostate)
Atherosclerosis of internal pudendal or penile arteries
Erectile dysfunction, often an early sign of systemic vascular disease
Autonomic nerves and endothelial nitric oxide
Retroperitoneal node dissection injuring sympathetic chain or hypogastric plexus
Alpha-1 blockade or surgery at the bladder neck
blocks.caption: Retrograde ejaculation is confirmed mechanistically by sperm in urine collected after orgasm.

blocks.text: The female response follows the same plan: parasympathetic S2 to S4 fibers dilate vessels of the clitoris and vestibular bulbs and increase vaginal transudation (lubrication), while orgasmic contractions of the perineal muscles are carried by the pudendal nerve.

blocks.predict: Predict the sexual function deficit after injury to the superior hypogastric plexus during retroperitoneal lymph node dissection.
blocks.explain: Erection (sacral parasympathetic) and the pudendal nerve are spared, but sympathetic emission and bladder neck closure are lost.

sections.title: Course of the pudendal nerve and the ischial spine landmark

blocks.text: The pudendal nerve is the main somatic nerve of the perineum. It forms from the ventral rami of S2 to S4 in the sacral plexus and carries sensation from the perineal skin, motor fibers to the striated perineal muscles and external sphincters, and sympathetic fibers to perineal skin. Its route is indirect: it leaves the pelvis, hooks around the ischial spine, and re-enters below the pelvic floor, because the perineum lies beneath the levator ani and the nerve cannot reach it by passing straight through.

blocks.title: Course of the pudendal nerve
steps: Ventral rami of S2 to S4 join in the sacral plexus
Exits pelvis through greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis
Crosses the sacrospinous ligament at the ischial spine
Re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen
Runs in the pudendal canal on obturator internus fascia
Divides into inferior rectal, perineal, and dorsal nerves
blocks.caption: The internal pudendal artery and vein take the same route, lying alongside the nerve at the ischial spine.

blocks.text: At the ischial spine the nerve lies on the posterior surface of the sacrospinous ligament, near its attachment to the spine, with the internal pudendal vessels beside it. The spine can be felt through the lateral vaginal wall, which makes it the landmark for a transvaginal pudendal nerve block during the second stage of labor. Anesthetic placed just medial and posterior to the spine bathes the nerve before it enters the pudendal canal. The canal itself is a split in the obturator fascia on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa.

blocks.title: Branches of the pudendal nerve
rows: Perianal skin and anal canal below the pectinate line
Bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, transverse perineal muscles, external urethral sphincter
Dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris
Skin of the penis or clitoris, especially the glans
blocks.caption: The pudendal nerve carries both sensation and continence, so its injury causes both numbness and sphincter weakness.

blocks.text: A pudendal block numbs most of the perineum but has clear limits that follow from other nerves. Pain from uterine contractions travels with sympathetic fibers to about T10 to L1 and is untouched. The anterior labia are supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, and part of the posterior perineum by the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, so sensation may persist there.

Injury follows the course. Prolonged or difficult vaginal delivery stretches the nerve where it is fixed at the ischial spine and in the pudendal canal, and long periods of cycling compress it in the canal or between the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments. The result is perineal numbness or burning pain, worse when sitting, with possible weakness of the external anal and urethral sphincters that contributes to fecal and stress urinary incontinence.

sections.title: Blood supply and lymph drainage of the breast

blocks.text: The breast lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the pectoralis major and part of the serratus anterior, extending as an axillary tail toward the armpit. It has no arteries of its own and is supplied by the vessels that run beside it. Medially, perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery (from the subclavian) emerge through the second to fourth intercostal spaces. Laterally, the lateral thoracic artery and pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery, both from the axillary artery, enter the gland. Lateral branches of the posterior intercostal arteries in the second to fourth spaces add to the supply.

Veins follow the arteries to the axillary vein, internal thoracic veins, and intercostal veins. The intercostal veins connect with the valveless vertebral venous plexus, which offers tumor cells a route to the vertebrae that bypasses the lungs.

blocks.title: Breast arteries
rows: Perforating (medial mammary) branches of internal thoracic
Lateral branches of posterior intercostals (spaces 2 to 4)
blocks.caption: Arteries enter from the medial and lateral sides, so the gland has a rich collateral supply.

blocks.text: Lymph collects in a plexus under the areola and in the gland and then follows the arteries. More than about 75% drains, mainly from the lateral quadrants, to the axillary nodes, usually first to the pectoral (anterior) group. From there lymph passes to central and apical nodes, then to the subclavian lymphatic trunk and supraclavicular nodes. Most of the remainder, mainly from the medial quadrants, runs with the perforating vessels to the parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic artery. Smaller routes reach the opposite breast and, from the inferior quadrants, the abdominal wall below the diaphragm.

blocks.title: Main lymph route from the lateral breast
steps: Subareolar and glandular lymphatic plexus
Pectoral (anterior) axillary nodes
Central axillary nodes
Apical axillary nodes
Subclavian lymphatic trunk and supraclavicular nodes
Venous angle at the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins
blocks.caption: This stepwise route is why axillary nodes are usually the first site of breast cancer spread and why a single sentinel node can represent the axilla.

blocks.text: These routes predict spread and its signs. A lateral tumor usually reaches axillary nodes first, while a medial tumor can reach parasternal nodes that lie inside the chest wall, beyond the axilla. When tumor cells block dermal lymphatics, the skin swells around tethered hair follicles and looks pitted like orange peel (peau d'orange); this is the hallmark of inflammatory carcinoma. Tumor involving the suspensory ligaments shortens them and dimples the skin. Removing axillary nodes interrupts lymph return from the arm and can cause lymphedema, and the long thoracic nerve on the serratus anterior lies in the same field, so its injury produces a winged scapula.

integration.text: Embryology explains the vessels: the gonads arise near the kidneys and descend, so their arteries, veins, and lymph still run to the aorta, IVC, left renal vein, and para-aortic nodes, while pelvic organs that never moved are supplied from the internal iliac system. Physiology explains why vessel anatomy matters: the pampiniform plexus is a heat exchanger, so venous congestion becomes a fertility problem, and erection is a nitric oxide and cGMP event that depends on both nerves and endothelium, linking sexual function to diabetes and atherosclerosis. Autonomic organization explains the male sexual response, and somatic sacral segments explain continence and perineal sensation.

Pathology applies these routes to spread. Following the artery back to its source predicts the first nodal station for testicular, ovarian, cervical, vulvar, scrotal, and breast tumors, but the rule has limits: the uterus drains partly along the round ligament to the groin, midline vulvar lesions can drain to both sides, ovarian cancer spreads mainly across the peritoneum, and prior surgery or skin invasion can open new lymphatic routes. Individual variation in arterial origins and nodal anatomy is common, so these patterns predict the usual case rather than every patient.

summary: Gonadal arteries arise from the aorta at about L2 because the gonads descend from the upper lumbar region; the ovarian artery anastomoses with the uterine artery.
The right gonadal vein enters the IVC obliquely; the longer left vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, so about 90% of varicoceles are left-sided.
A varicocele that does not empty when supine, or appears suddenly or only on the right, suggests venous obstruction such as a renal tumor or IVC obstruction.

The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac and crosses above the ureter about 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix, where clamping can ligate, cut, or devascularize the ureter.
Testis and ovary drain to para-aortic nodes; uterus, cervix, and upper vagina to iliac nodes; scrotum, vulva, and lower vagina to superficial inguinal nodes.

Erection is parasympathetic (S2 to S4, nitric oxide, cGMP, veno-occlusion), emission is sympathetic (about T11 to L2, alpha-1, bladder neck closure), and ejaculation is somatic (pudendal, bulbospongiosus).
Loss of sympathetic bladder neck closure causes retrograde ejaculation; cavernous nerve or arterial injury causes erectile dysfunction.

The pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) leaves through the greater sciatic foramen, crosses the sacrospinous ligament at the ischial spine, and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen to the pudendal canal.
The ischial spine is the landmark for pudendal block, which numbs the perineum but not uterine contraction pain (T10 to L1).

The breast is supplied by internal thoracic, lateral thoracic, thoracoacromial, and posterior intercostal arteries; over about 75% of its lymph goes to axillary nodes, with medial quadrants also draining to parasternal nodes.

verify: The distance at which the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery is quoted from about 1 to 2.5 cm lateral to the cervix in different texts; this chapter uses about 1.5 to 2 cm.
Spinal levels for sympathetic outflow to the reproductive tract are given as T10 to L2, T11 to L2, or L1 to L2 in different sources; this chapter uses about T11 to L2.
The proportion of varicoceles on the left (about 90%) and the prevalence in adult men (about 15%) are approximate consensus figures; confirm the values NABNE expects.
The share of breast lymph reaching axillary nodes is quoted as more than 75% (Moore) and up to about 97% in some surgical series; confirm the figure NABNE expects.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponym Alcock canal and the mnemonic phrases "water under the bridge" and "point, squeeze, and shoot"; this chapter uses descriptive terms only.
Lymph from the glans penis and clitoris is described as going to deep inguinal nodes in Moore and to superficial and deep inguinal nodes in other texts.
